info.desc: Wasting Light is the seventh studio album by American rock band Foo Fighters, released April 12, 2011, by Roswell and RCA. It's their first album to feature guitarist Pat Smear since The Colour and the Shape (1997); he appeared on their previous album, Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace (2007), as a session musician only. Wanting to capture the essence of their earlier work and avoid the artificiality of digital recording, Foo Fighters recorded in the garage of frontman Dave Grohl in Encino, California, using only analog equipment. The sessions were produced by the band alongside Butch Vig, with whom Grohl had worked on Nirvana's Nevermind (1991). Since the old equipment did not allow for many mistakes to be corrected .

podcast.body: Despite the Foo Fighters being a major band and "Wasting Light" being their best-selling album of the 2010s, it only ranked as the 50th best-selling rock album of the decade on a general list. This illustrates the declining importance of albums and rock music's lower sales performance compared to other genres during the streaming era. "Despite being as big and as famous as they are, their 2011 album Wasting Light was the best selling of the decade. And on a list of the top selling rock albums of the decade, it clocked in at just number fifty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released after a four-year hiatus, the 2011 album "Wasting Light" was uniquely recorded in Dave Grohl's garage in 2012, eschewing expensive modern studios for old analog equipment and the production expertise of Butch Vig, known for Nirvana's "Nevermind." This decision reflected Dave Grohl's desire for a primal, raw, and old-school sound, with edits made using razor blades and a backyard tent serving as the control room, and no digital processes until mastering. The recording process famously reunited three key figures from Nirvana's "Nevermind" – Dave Grohl, Butch Vig, and bassist Krist Novoselic, who played on the song "I Should Have Known." "There was absolutely nothing digital about this album until the mastering process. No computers. It was old school analog with ancient tape recorders all the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
